analysis.one_liner: Bars companies and data brokers from collecting or selling personal reproductive and sexual health information.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 119 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit companies outside the doctor-patient system from collecting, keeping, or sharing personal reproductive or sexual health data — including period-tracker information, pregnancy status, searches for abortion services, and location data suggesting such visits — unless it is strictly needed to provide the service the person asked for. It would give people the right to see, correct, and delete that data, require clear privacy policies, and let both the Federal Trade Commission and individuals enforce the rules, with damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation per day. It would also bar companies from forcing users into arbitration over these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses period trackers, fertility apps, pregnancy tests, telehealth services, or simply searches for reproductive health care. After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, this kind of data can be bought by third parties and sought in investigations or lawsuits over abortion in states where it is banned. The bill would sharply shrink the pool of data available for that purpose and give individuals direct control over it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People using period, fertility, and health apps

how_it_helps.text: Companies may collect, retain, use, or disclose reproductive or sexual health information only when strictly necessary to provide the product or service the user requested [S2].

Individuals gain enforceable rights to access, correct, and delete their reproductive health data — including data inferred by algorithms or bought from third parties — with a 15-day compliance deadline and no fees [S2].
Companies must publish detailed privacy policies listing exactly which third parties they sell such data to and why [S2].

Violations are enforceable by the FTC and by individuals in court, with $100–$1,000 per violation per day or actual damages, attorney's fees, and invalidation of pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers [S2].
The bill does not preempt stronger state privacy laws and carves out entities already covered by HIPAA, so it targets the unregulated app and data-broker market rather than doctor's offices [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Apps and websites that monetize reproductive health data — period and fertility trackers, digital advertisers, and data brokers — would lose a source of revenue and face compliance costs and lawsuit exposure. Consumers might see more friction, such as privacy prompts, or in rare cases apps dropping features that require sensitive data.
analysis.who_pays_short: Period apps, data brokers, and ad networks

drawbacks.text: The private right of action allows $100–$1,000 per violation per day plus attorney's fees, which critics of similar laws warn can produce costly class-action litigation over technical compliance slip-ups [S2].

The definition of covered data is extremely broad — including location information that 'might indicate' an attempt to obtain reproductive services and any algorithmically inferred data — which small app developers could find difficult to apply with certainty [S2].

Companies already covered by HIPAA are excluded, so the bill would not tighten the rules governing data held by hospitals, insurers, and clinics — only the large consumer-data market outside them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: it removes a specific, documented risk in which commercial data about pregnancies and abortion searches can be obtained by third parties and law enforcement after Dobbs. The costs fall on a narrow set of companies profiting from that data, plus some litigation risk from broad damages provisions. A fair reading is that the protections outweigh the compliance burden, though the breadth of the definitions and the damages formula would likely need refinement in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 17, 2023 by Rep. Sara Jacobs with 118 original cosponsors [S1].
On May 17 it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on May 19 to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
The cosponsor list grew to 119, all Democrats, with no Republican support [S3].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history for the remainder of the Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, advertisers, and app companies keep collecting and selling reproductive health data with no new federal restrictions. No consumer protections took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and tracking apps that keep selling data

industries.note: These companies buy, infer, and resell signals about pregnancies, contraception, and abortion searches. The bill's strict minimization rule and deletion rights would cut off much of that trade, which currently happens outside HIPAA with no federal limits [S2].

industries.industry: Period-tracking, fertility, and reproductive health app developers
industries.note: Apps whose core service depends on menstrual or pregnancy data could keep collecting what is strictly necessary, but could no longer monetize it through third parties and would face access, deletion, and privacy-policy duties plus lawsuit exposure [S2].

industries.industry: Hospitals, doctors, and HIPAA-covered health providers
industries.note: The bill excludes HIPAA-covered entities, leaving health providers operating under existing medical-privacy rules and making the non-medical app and broker market the target [S2].
